title: Ulysses (Joyce, 1922)

Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the epiphany and the open ending (Dubliners).
historical_context: The Dublin and Paris of the 1900s, the Irish lyric tradition and the fin-de-siècle aesthetic of the young Joyce. The record dates the work as composed between 1901 and 1904 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line.

title: Prufrock and Other Observations
description: The first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady' and the urban lyric. It is a verse work of 1917 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under modernist lyric and the new idiom; dramatic monologue and masked lyric and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady', 'Preludes', 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night', 'Aunt Helen' and 'The Boston Evening Transcript' — the poems of the modern city, the anti-heroic voice and the ironic quotation that founded English modernism.
narrative_structure: Twelve poems in free verse and irregular rhyme. A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: J. Alfred Prufrock; the lady of the portrait; the women who come and go
literary_form: Poetry collection (published by the Egoist Press)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
historical_context: The Boston and London of the 1910s, the drawing rooms of the American aesthete, and the new urban consciousness of the modern city. The record dates the work as composed between 1911 and 1915 and first published in 1917 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom; dramatic monologue and masked lyric.
literary_significance: Prufrock and Other Observations is the first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' made the anti-heroic voice the central instrument of modern poetry, and 'Preludes' and 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night' invented the modern urban lyric.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by the Egoist in London in June 1917 in an edition of 500 copies, with an introduction by Ezra Pound. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Waste Land
description: The central poem of modernism: five sections of fragments, quotation and myth, and the modern world as a waste land. It is a verse work of 1922 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under modernist long poem and the mythical method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with 'April is the cruellest month' and moves through the burial of the dead, the game of chess, the fire sermon, the death by water and 'What the Thunder Said': a collage of voices — Marie in the Hofgarten, the hyacinth girl, Madame Sosostris, Tiresias, the typist and the young man carbuncular, Phlebas the Phoenician — held together by the myth of the Fisher King and the search for rain.
narrative_structure: Five sections (The Burial of the Dead, A Game of Chess, The Fire Sermon, Death by Water, What the Thunder Said), 433 lines.
principal_characters: Tiresias; Madame Sosostris; Marie; the hyacinth girl; the typist; the young man carbuncular; Phlebas
literary_form: Long poem (five sections; first published in The Criterion, October 1922)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
historical_context: Post-war London and Europe after 1918, the collapse of the old order, the Russian Revolution, and the anthropology of Frazer's Golden Bough and Weston's From Ritual to Romance, which Eliot cites in his notes.
literary_significance: The Waste Land is the central poem of modernism and the most influential poem of the century: its collage of quotation and mythic parallel created the modern long poem, its notes made allusion a public technique, and its vision of a civilisation in fragments defined the period's imagination. Pound's editing of the manuscript is the most famous act of modernist collaboration.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Drafted 1921 and cut by Ezra Pound from a much longer manuscript; published in The Criterion (October 1922) and The Dial (November 1922), then by Boni and Liveright (New York, December 1922) with Eliot's notes. The manuscript was published in facsimile in 1971.

title: Four Quartets
alternative_titles: Four Quartets: Burnt Norton, East Coker, The Dry Salvages, Little Gidding
description: Eliot's great religious poem: time, memory and the still point of the turning world. It is a verse work of 1943 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under modernist long poem and the mythical method; verse drama and the poetic play and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The four poems — 'Burnt Norton' (1936), 'East Coker' (1940), 'The Dry Salvages' (1941), 'Little Gidding' (1942) — each in five movements, meditate on time, place, history and the possibility of incarnation. The sequence moves from a Gloucestershire rose garden to the village of Eliot's ancestors, to the Mississippi and the sea, to a bombed London street, and closes with 'the fire and the rose are one'.
narrative_structure: Four poems of five movements each, built on the analogy of the late Beethoven quartets. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
principal_characters: the speaker; the familiar compound ghost ('Little Gidding')
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.

The record dates the work as composed between 1935 and 1942 and first published in 1943 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; verse drama and the poetic play.
literary_significance: Four Quartets is the greatest English religious poem of the century and the summit of Eliot's achievement: it turned the modernist fragment into a sustained meditation on time, history and redemption and made the wartime London of the Blitz part of its structure.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: The four poems were published separately: Burnt Norton (Faber and Faber, in Collected Poems 1909-1935, 1936), East Coker (Faber, May 1940), The Dry Salvages (Faber, February 1941) and Little Gidding (Faber, October 1942); the sequence was first issued as a single volume by Faber and Faber in 1944. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Ash-Wednesday
description: Eliot's conversion poem: the turn from despair to faith, and the most penitential poem in modern English. It is a verse work of 1930 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under modernist long poem and the mythical method; verse drama and the poetic play and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves from the speaker's refusal of hope and his ascent of the purgatorial stairs, through the vision of the lady and the yew trees, to the prayer for intercession that closes it.
narrative_structure: Six sections of varying length, with the refrain of the Lady and the yew trees. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
principal_characters: the speaker; the Lady; the silent sister veiled in white and blue
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
historical_context: Eliot's baptism and confirmation in the Church of England in 1927, and his Anglo-Catholic faith of the late 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1929 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; verse drama and the poetic play.

title: Murder in the Cathedral
alternative_titles: Murder in the Cathedral: A Play with Chorus
description: Eliot's verse drama of the martyrdom of Thomas Becket: the great modern verse play in English. It is a dramatic work of 1935 by T. S. Eliot; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under verse drama and the poetic play and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The Chorus of the Women of Canterbury, the three priests and the four tempters prepare for the archbishop's return; Becket refuses the tempters' offers of power, pleasure, political action and martyrdom itself, preaches his Christmas sermon on the paradox of the martyr, and is murdered in the cathedral by the four knights, who then address the audience directly.
narrative_structure: Two parts, with a chorus, a sermon and the murder as the climax. A play in acts in verse, the poetic line carrying the dialogue and the lyric and choral passages set apart.
principal_characters: Thomas Becket; the Chorus of the Women of Canterbury; the three priests; the four tempters; the four knights
literary_form: Verse play (first performed in Canterbury Cathedral, 1935)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama: the poetic line, blank verse or a regular stanza, carries the dialogue, and the play alternates the verse speech with lyric and choral passages. The author's characteristic manner is the abrupt juxtaposition of registers and quotations.
historical_context: The murder of Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170, and the political crisis of the 1930s, which made the play an allegory of the church against the totalitarian state. The record dates the work as composed in 1935 and first published in 1935 and first performed in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method, it is catalogued under verse drama and the poetic play.
literary_significance: Murder in the Cathedral is the great verse play of the period and the founding work of the modern revival of poetic drama: its chorus, ritual structure and analysis of the will made it a permanent work of the English stage.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Thomas Stearns Eliot. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Faber and Faber in May 1935, having been written for the Canterbury Festival and first performed in the Chapter House at Canterbury on 15 June 1935; the American edition of 1935 carries the title Murder in the Cathedral: A Play with Chorus. The record grades the work as major canon.
